MR. DEACHMAN-REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF PRESS RELEASE RESPECTING FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the publication of a story by me in the Ottawa Citizen yesterday a few minutes before the report of the flag committee was tabled, and in view of what was said about that in the house yesterday, I respectfully request Your Honour to have this matter referred to the committee on privileges and elections.

subtopic: MR. DEACHMAN-REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF PRESS RELEASE RESPECTING FLAG COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra made a suggestion to the house, but it would require an order of the house to carry out that suggestion. Before any action is taken one way or the other I feel it my duty to make one or two points.
It is undoubtedly a very serious thing to attack the conduct of any member of the House of Commons, and in that respect a specific charge should always be made, not a general charge. I am confirmed in this opinion by an excellent ruling, it seems to me, given by Mr. Speaker Michener on June 19, 1959, which appears at pages 583 and 584 of the Journals. I should like to refer to two short sentences in that ruling. I read from page 583:
It has been strongly urged by some members that the house should not set in motion its power to try and to judge the conduct of a member unless such member is charged with a specific offence. It is urged further that not only must he be charged, but that he must be charged by a member of the House of Commons standing in his place.
These are the words of Mr. Speaker Michener:
In my view, simple justice requires that no honourable member should have to submit to investigation of his conduct by the house or a committee until he has been charged with an offence.
Later on the same page, 584, I read:
In the case before us no honourable member has taken the responsibility of making a specific charge against the honourable member for Peel.
The practice in the Canadian House of Commons, up to the present, has been to give notice of intention. Of course a true question of privilege can be raised at any time, but it should be raised immediately. It seems to me that the matter was referred to yesterday in fairly strong terms, and under the heading of "earliest opportunity" I think it conforms, in view of my statement that I was taken by surprise and would look into the matter.
The role of the Speaker is outlined in Beauchesne, citation 104, subsection 2. I must say that, accordingly, if the house wishes to refer this matter to the committee on privileges and elections, so be it. In my opinion it should not be concerned with the conduct of the member but should be more of an investigation into the matter. However, that is up to the house to decide. Since there is nothing before the Chair, I suggest that if it is the desire to look into this matter an order of the house should issue.
Is it the pleasure of the house to refer this matter to the committee on privileges and elections?

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. 5. Pearson (Prime Minister):
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the house to an event which has for all of us its element of sadness, as I am sure it has for the gentleman concerned, although perhaps there is also an element of release and anticipation. I refer to the fact that this is the last day our Clerk Assistant, Mr. Montgomery, will be in his chair in the House of Commons.
Mr. Montgomery joined the public service in 1912 and entered the service of the House of Commons in 1915. He is in his fiftieth year of service to the house. With his service to the house he has combined other forms of public service, community service, civil service, war charities and war activities, and for all this over so many years we owe him a debt of gratitude which I am sure we are all very proud and happy to acknowledge this morning. We thank him for what he has done in the public service of Canada, and we wish him many years of happiness and enjoyment ahead.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of those times when there is unity in the House of Commons as we do an unusual honour to one who has devoted his life to the public service. The Prime Minister has spoken in detail of that service. All of us who have sat in this chamber know what Mr. Montgomery's contribution has meant. He has been kindly, courteous and always devoted to the welfare of those in this chamber. There will be universal regret that after a half century of service he is about to retire.
We have no means of showing our appreciation for those that serve us well. We have no decoration such as the Victorian Order in the United Kingdom, which permits the

sovereign on behalf of the nation to show the appreciation of the nation. We take this means of saying to Mr. Montgomery how deeply grateful we have been, and indeed are, to him and to all those who serve us in this chamber in the capacity of Clerk, Clerk Assistant and the other officials who give of their best to their country. Too often we do not pay tribute to civil servants who serve us so well. This is one occasion when, through Mr. Montgomery, we can pay our tribute not only to him in affection, but also to all those who serve in the civil service in devotion to their country.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think you and all hon. members will realize that had it not been for the top priority afforded the Prime Minister I should have risen in my place and spoken to a question of privilege on this day, which is a sad occasion for this House of Commons.
All of us are aware of the loyalty and ability Mr. Montgomery as Clerk Assistant has given to the House of Commons collectively and to members individually. In order to complete the record of Mr. Montgomery's services I should like to add to the words of the right hon. Prime Minister, and record in Hansard the fact that Mr. Montgomery, the Clerk Assistant of this house, has been a federal civil servant for fifty years and four months. Added to that record is the astounding fact that he has been an employee of the House of Commons for forty-nine years and three months, and for the past 13 years has been Clerk Assistant.
In addition to these services Mr. Montgomery has accepted other responsibilities from time to time. He has had a keen interest in and knowledge of the commonwealth parliamentary association. For the past 13 years he has been either assistant secretary or secretary of that association. I doubt whether there is any man in the commonwealth, except perhaps at the head office in London, who knows more of the details about that association and its work.
Although Mr. Montgomery today is resigning from his position as Clerk Assistant, we in the commonwealth parliamentary association are very pleased that at our last executive meeting he offered to continue his services and lend his knowledge to the work that association must do, commencing next month, in preparing for the commonwealth parliamentary association conference which will be held in

Canada in 1967. I am sure I express the appreciation and gratitude of all of us to Mr. Montgomery, who has informed the executive of the C.P.A. of his availability. That offer demonstrates just why we hold him in such aifection and believe that although retiring from one position, he will yet be available to serve Canada in years to come.
On behalf of this group, sir, I add our expression of good will and our wishes for his good health and his opportunity to serve Canada for many years ahead.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a genuine pleasure to be able to say a few words in support of the remarks made by the Prime Minister and representatives of the other parties with regard to our respected and beloved fellow worker in the House of Commons, Mr. Montgomery. In the few short years it has been my privilege to be a member of the house I have come to appreciate in a very special way his constant and continual friendly helpfulness. This applies not only to his official responsibilities, but has been carried over so many times beyond the normal call of duty to little things that he was under no obligation to do.
I think this is one of the reasons those of us who have come to know him on that basis refer to him affectionately as "Monty." We regard him as more than just a fellow worker and friend. We regard him as what he truly is, a devoted and dedicated public servant and citizen of Canada.
On behalf of myself personally as well as the other members of our group may I say that he is certainly worthy of all the kindly words that have been uttered, and the brevity of my remarks in no way reflects the depth of our appreciation for him. We appreciate the fact that he is going to continue to be with us. We join in the remarks that have just been made with regard to the tremendous contribution he has made to the commonwealth parliamentary association, and we are indeed pleased that in serving that important organization he will continue to be with us.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO CLERK ASSISTANT ON RETIREMENT
speechtext:

We, members of the Ralliement Creditiste, also wish to Mr. Montgomery many years of

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked me a question about the conference on Indian affairs which is now taking place. I have had this question looked into, and am informed that several individuals objected to the holding of this conference without Indian representation and that a telegram was received from the president of the native brotherhood of British Columbia by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration on October 28, the evening before the conference started. Mr. Williams, the president, in effect said that the conference was a step in the right direction, but that it would be wrong and undemocratic for any agreement to be reached between the federal and provincial governments without the British Columbia Indians participating. He said the Indians must be consulted and fully informed. That is also the position of the federal government.
The purpose of this conference is to discover-and this is its only purpose, or an important one-whether it is possible for the federal government to formulate programs with each of the provinces for submission to Indians and consideration by them. If it is found as a result of this conference that progress can be made in bringing services needed in Indian communities through provincial facilities, then the matter will be discussed with the Indians. The federal government has made clear, and I am glad to confirm this, that at each step the Indians must be consulted in advance of changes which affect them in any way.

Mr. Chairman, during the last few days in committee of supply we have been talking about the C.B.C. Yesterday I attempted to discuss another problem, but I was ruled out of order. Today I wish to change the subject somewhat.
Hear, hear.

I am pleased to be met with such approval, and I hope that approval will remain throughout the remarks I intend to make. One of the most striking questions

which face this nation today is whether we are going to retain the kind of strong central government which the Fathers of Confederation planned when this country became a union of four nations, or four provinces, in 1867.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
I have hardly got started, but if you have a question I will try to answer it.

Am I to understand the hon. member is a supporter of the compact theory of confederation, which seemed to have been disposed of by the late Hon. Norman Rogers in the 1930's? Am I to further understand that the hon. member is suggesting that there were four nations which joined together in 1867? Is the hon. member not aware that the union between Ontario and Quebec preceded that event by some 25 years?

I do not intend to get into an argument about constitutional law with my good friend, but I am always very interested in his questions. I am sure if he listens to the address I have prepared he will understand what I feel should be taking place in reference to a strong central government in Ottawa. Perhaps I should answer his question in this way. I do not believe this nation can survive if we are to have ten balkan states. We cannot exist with the kind of loose network of federalism which has been perpetuated by this government.
The present government makes reference to co-operative federalism. I believe it was this party which actually coined that expression. Unfortunately coined words are used in different ways. This government is placing a different interpretation on that coined expression than was intended. The charge I make is that the Pearson government is Canada's assassin, and that you are all honorary pallbearers to this nation. I did not intend to get into that type of address immediately but did so because of the question the hon. member posed.
Canada is still a very young nation made up of people with many cultures and traditions. The population in western Canada, which is made up of people of many ethnic origins, feel very deeply about this fact. They realize that this nation was created by people who came to this land from all the countries of Europe and Asia with deep rooted hatred and prejudice toward one another. These prejudices, hatreds and animosities were the
Interim Supply
result of European wars fought by their fathers and grandfathers. One could perhaps say that in Europe the Germans hated the French, the British disliked them both, while the Russians disliked all three.
These people came to Canada in search of a new nation and a new destiny with these prejudices, animosities and hatreds buried in their hearts and bosoms. They found, whether they settled in villages, towns or on farms, and whatever avocations the neighbours over the back fences had chosen, be they German, English, French or of another ethnic origin, they were the same kind of people. These people realized that the neighbours had different cultures, traditions and backgrounds, but they had also come to Canada in search of a new destiny, and that they were all friends after all.
The most important thing we must keep in mind in dealing with a nation is that these prejudices and animosities were buried long ago. I believe Canada was the first country to legislate in respect of freedom of religion. I think Canada did so even before Great Britain and other countries, who are looked upon as the mothers of liberty and freedom.
Oh, oh.

Surely the hon. member is not going to take the position that the rules of law and tradition we inherited from the Anglo Saxon system are bad. I have always maintained that the rules of law we have in our democracy represent the kind of freedoms that all Canadians enjoy. We do enjoy these freedoms because of those rules of law. A very simple example can be found in the fact that our children can leave their homes, whether they be in Scarborough, Calgary or Montreal, travel to school and return home safely. That is the case not because of the efforts of any one province but because of the protection given to individuals by the rules of law against infringement by the state or other individuals.
Many people feel that Canada is a union of two nations. If they mean that this nation is a union of two great cultures and traditions I agree completely. If they mean that this nation is a union of two completely different states, then I cannot agree. It is now a union of ten provinces. Canada began as a union of four provinces, whether that union took place ten years or 25 years after a union between two provinces. The nation finally became a union of ten provinces.
That is the kind of country we have, but I say that if we are now to weaken the very fabric of confederation by taking away the

powers of the strong, central federal government we will end up as 10 nations, 10 balkan-ized states, and the nation will finally dissolve.
You are exaggerating.

My friend says I am exaggerating. He would know something about exaggeration, because he is a master of exaggeration and imagination. I do not want to get into an argument with him and perhaps he might bear with me. I have listened to his views, and I have learned a lot from the hon. member. I admit that he takes a different position from mine. I was born and raised in another province with a different culture. We who were born and raised in western Canada have our culture, our traditions and our heritage. Are we not permitted to present our arguments with regard to confederation? Is this not one Canada? Is the argument to be all one sided, with only one doctrine preached and not both sides of the picture? How can we ever hold the country together in that way? If we all think alike there is no thinking. That is my answer to that hon. member.
Let us take a look at what has really gone on. I say and I really believe that the present government-this may be strong language- has been Canada's assassin and is now acting as honorary pallbearer at its funeral.
Oh, well-

Somebody says "oh, well". I want to say this afternoon-it is afternoon by now-that in the minds of the people of western Canada this government has been playing the grasshopper game. What do I mean by that? The two great players in this game are the present Prime Minister and Mr. Lesage. They are the players in the grasshopper game, and they hop in and hop out of certain federal economic programs.
We have some proven programs. We have the winter works program, the vocational training program, even unemployment insurance. Let us deal with unemployment insurance. When it was first brought before the House of Commons in the days of R. B. Bennett it was charged that the act was unconstitutional, but after an amendment to the constitution unemployment insurance finally became the law and applied to all Canadians.
I am going to have something to say about the British North America Act itself, but surely under confederation those things that apply to all Canadians and are common to all of us, those things which are not of local

concern to the province of Quebec or Alberta or Ontario, are national in scope. Sometimes we have had to get agreement on the part of the provinces because of the wording of the act, but I say that any federal government that makes deals with Mr. Lesage or any other premier to hop in and out of economic programs which have already been proven is an assassin of the country and is acting as honorary pallbearer at its funeral.

speechtext: Those words will come back to you.

I hear my friend saying something. The Liberals do not like what I am saying because they know it is true. I want to deal with my second point, the constitution itself. A question was put to the Prime Minister yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition, and the Prime Minister, I believe, answered that there was no change in the new formula for amendment of the constitution from that sponsored by Hon. Davie Fulton, the former minister of justice.
I say that is untrue. It is not intellectually correct and it is not legally correct. I see the Minister of Transport looking at me. I do not say any more than that. I do not think the Prime Minister deliberately got up and gave a false opinion. I do say you will find that intellectually there is a difference in the formula. That is my first charge.
The hon. gentleman has put a question to me, and if he will give me the page I should like to answer it. Could the hon. gentleman give me the page in Hansard?
I may be thinking of another question, but that is the way it seemed to me yesterday.
I listened to the Prime Minister, and I would rather read exactly what he said.
Let us read what he said.
If somebody can find the page faster than I can-

I do not want to give any interpretation. I want to read it.

If the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wants to make a speech

when I am finished and contradict me, let him do so. He was going to ask a question. I do not think he has risen on a question of privilege. I thought I had permission but, of course, if the hon. gentleman does not want me to-
Would the minister then be prepared to agree to the extension of my time by the amount of my time he is taking now?

Fine.

Here is what the Prime Minister said, Mr. Chairman, as found on page 9547 of Hansard:

He was referring to the delegation of federal powers to the provinces. On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might be allowed to apologize to the hon. gentleman. I was not implying for one minute that he was not competent to read. I was just suggesting that perhaps he had not yet had the time to do so.

Again we have sarcasm and we have the boys who laugh at the sarcasm. I will answer in this vein. Say something intelligent.

This is my answer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I have not checked this, but when this matter was first brought before the house it was my interpretation of the Prime Minister's language that he meant

that in a day or two this matter would be debated and quickly approved because the 10 provincial premiers had approved it and the government had approved it.
But this is too serious a matter for that kind of treatment. That is why a member of the New Democratic party quite properly rose and said they were going to fight it. constitution. It is through these powers that parliament operates.
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would allow me to ask him a question.
I wonder if I can finish my remarks, please.

I do not want to be rude, but I have hurt my friend's feelings. If he will bear with me, I should like to hear what he has to say when I have completed my remarks. As I say, I should like to get him on record about this matter.
I should like to make my personal recommendation to the government right now. I have a deep suspicion-and I think this is why the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate keeps asking me questions-that under the guise of bringing home the constitution we are in danger of weakening the powers of the central government and dividing up this country into ten balkan states. You, sir, give in to the separatists of the province of Quebec.
Now you are starting to divide Canada.

I hear some of them shouting about the province of Quebec. I believe this, and I will say it not only in this house but elsewhere; I believe the people of Quebec want a strong country just as those in any other part of the nation do. It is time that we spoke up like leaders instead of trying to soft soap the whole problem we have in this country. You are never going to cure the patient by giving him these weak soda pills. There were certain powers delegated to the central government, and certain powers delegated to the provinces. This party has been on record for years in favour of bringing the constitution home so that Canada can attain full nationhood in every respect. I am in favour of it, and this party has been in favour of it. I believe everyone in Canada

is in favour of it. If under the guise of bringing home the constitution, because everybody is so happy to see it come home, we carve up and destroy this nation, then I say to the Liberal party that the responsibility rests on their shoulders. You are the assassins of this country.
When they talk about separatists they laugh. We do not even have to go to the province of Quebec to find separatists now. This is his latest pronouncement made in Montreal. He was going down to Montreal to appease these people to whom this government will not say no and to whom this government should say no. If the government of Alberta, even though it is my home province, wanted to do something which was detrimental to this country I should hope this government would exercise the kind of responsibility it should exercise, and say no. The whole question of the revision of the constitution poses rather special problems for 50,000 of our northern people who happen to live in the Yukon and Northwest Territories because neither the Yukon nor the Northwest Territories is in confederation yet. As hon. members are probably aware, when the responsibilities and tax fields that were

to be divided were defined in the British North America Act only two spheres were envisaged, the federal sphere and the provincial sphere. The transitional stage of being a territory was meant to be precisely that, transitional, and I think it is most important that at this time when we are talking about repatriating the constitution the situation in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories should be reviewed rather carefully. It is even more important at this time, because neither of these territories was represented at the conference of attorneys general held recently to consider these matters.
I have listened attentively and quietly, Mr. Chairman, all afternoon to the remarks made by other members in the course of this debate and I would recommend to the hon. member for Lapointe that he should do the same. I too am concerned about the piecemeal dismemberment of this country at the hands of the Prime Minister and I do not hesitate to say that he must take full responsibility. He is supposed to be the leader of the government, although whether or not he is is something for him to worry about. But certainly we have seen the federal authority purposely weakened by his actions at a time when more than anything else we need a strong central government.
I know that the background of the Prime Minister is certainly an interesting and distinguished one in terms of his work at the United Nations. No one would question that the present Prime Minister was a great United Nations man, but although he may have been a great UN man he is certainly unable or unwilling to provide the kind of federal leadership that is required at the present time. This is the worst possible time for Canada to have a windsock prime minister. I am sure those of you who do any flying know what I mean when I refer to a windsock administration that turns in response to whichever way the breeze is blowing. This kind of approach to our problems is a source of real concern to me as the member for the Northwest Territories and to my colleague, the hon. member for Yukon, because if the Prime Minister insists on calling conference after conference at which the whole federal pie is put up for grabs, then those people who live in areas that are weaker in terms of their representation, either provincially or territorially, are going to be left with little more than crumbs.
There is another reason why I feel the situation within the two territories is serious. Right now neither the Yukon nor the North-

west Territories has full representation in parliament. If you will recall, Mr. Chairman, that parliament consists not only of the House of Commons but of the Queen and also the Senate, you will understand what I am driving at. At the present time neither the Yukon nor the Northwest Territories is represented in the Senate. There are no senators from either of these territories.
Some may automatically ask why we do not have such representation, or why we should have, in view of the sparse population of these areas. I am aware of the historical reasons for Prince Edward Island having four senators but I think it is fair to point out that at the present time more than 40,000 people live in the two northern territories. In my own constituency of the Northwest Territories we have over 26,000 people. Prince Edward Island, with a population of approximately 107,000, has four senators. As I say, I am aware of the historical reasons for this but I draw this matter to the attention of the committee, because in justice I think the two northern territories can insist on having representation in the Senate.
The previous administration made tremendous strides in opening up the Canadian north and embarked upon a program that concerned not only physical resource development, involving such things as airports, roads and railroads but which also gave the federal franchise to all residents of the Northwest Territories through the medium of the Nielsen bill, named after the hon. member for Yukon. This was part of a program to speed up the political development of Canada's far north, so that the logical step after the people were given elected representation in the House of Commons was to strengthen the local government and also to provide for the representation of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories in the other place.
The advantage of this sort of thing is surely obvious to anyone who will do a little thinking. It distresses me to see the Prime Minister deal away federal responsibilities in reaction to the slightest bit of pressure exerted upon him, but it is of particular concern because it tells those of us who live in the Canadian north that we may never get representation in the Senate.
The charge was made last week in Edmonton by the hon. member for Yukon and myself that for the past 18 months at any rate there has been a complete neglect of the affairs of the two northern territories, perhaps in retaliation for the northland having dared to send other than Liberal members to

this house or perhaps because of the traditional approach of the Liberal party which has been to neglect, to deride and overlook the needs of the rural areas of this country, whether they be in the west, the maritimes or the Canadian northland. In the past 18 months, there has not been a single new project initiated by the federal government in either of the two northern territories. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was in Edmonton and he talked about the wonderful railway that was now pushing the frontier up to latitude 62. He described this railway as the greatest single development in the Canadian northwest, and said it would be of even greater importance in the years ahead as the tremendous Pine Point lead and zinc deposits were exploited.
Fortunately, the Leader of the Opposition arrived in Edmonton on the same evening. He was quick to point out, and this was not lost to westerners, that every Liberal member in the House of Commons voted against the Pine Point railway at the time the bill was up for second reading. Now they are taking credit for this railway and saying what a wonderful thing it is. I mention these things, Mr. Chairman, not to thresh old straw, if you will, but because it is more crucial than ever for these two territories to rather quickly get representation in the Senate. This is a time when the creation of two positions in the other place for people from the north would be of great help. It is a time, perhaps because our territories are evolving very slowly, when the Senate, which is less involved in the day to day speculation about a general election and certainly does not need to be alarmed by partisanship in any of its strange forms, would be able to provide the sort of advice and study so necessary on behalf of the two northern territories. Now, in all the hundreds of thousands of words that have been spoken in this House of Commons in the last year in relation to solving problems, I have not heard a single member of the government refer to the fact that no provision was made to provide the Yukon and Northwest Territories with Senate representation.
The question I want answered is why this has happened? Surely, at a time when we are sitting down talking about making essential revisions, overdue revisions of the British North America Act, this is the logical time to plan an article in the constitution whereby the northern 50 per cent of this country can be brought under the British North America Act in a more meaningful way, and given full

representation in parliament. In late 1962 the hon. member for the Yukon was attempting to have this matter brought forward. At that time delay occurred because the development of political institutions in the Northwest Territories was proceeding apace. I do not believe anyone will quarrel with me seriously when I say it is more important for a resident of the northland to at least have the right to vote in federal elections, and it does not hurt to remind hon. members of this house that it was only in 1962 that every Canadian citizen over 21 years of age had the right to vote in federal elections. Prior to that time thousands of Canadians who were living in many parts of Canada's northland, whether they were Indian or Eskimo, were deprived of their vote. There was nothing in the election act that prevented them from voting, but they did not belong in any constituency. When the writs were issued and the lists were put up of the voters, tnere was nowhere they could vote.
There used to be a saying, when I was first knocking around the Northwest Territories, to the effect that if you wanted to lose your right to vote in Canada, all you had to do was to go to prison, go insane or go north. This situation was corrected. Not only were residents of the north given the federal franchise for the first time in June, 1962, but so were the Indian people. Prior to that time they did not have a franchise, because of their racial origin. When the accomplishments of the previous prime minister were being ridiculed and derided by the great exponent of political integrity, the Minister of Transport, to the jeers and catcalls of his loyal backbenchers, it was distressing to me to note that no one gave credit for this sort of thing. Yet, prior to the passage of the Canadian Bill of Rights and the implications that this had on the franchise in northern Canada, it was true that Canada had no right to hold up her head in the councils of the United Nations, at a time when many of her citizens were being deprived of the basic right to vote, solely because of their racial origin. I am speaking now of the Indian and Eskimo people. No one in this house knows what a tremendous step that was. If for nothing else, the previous prime minister deserves the commendation of Canadians and a place in history as the prime minister who, after 22 years of Liberal government, was the first to see that every Canadian citizen had the right to vote.

He said:

Mr. Speaker, as all hon. members know, the object of this bill is to bring the Senate abreast with the times we live in. There is no question of abolishing the Senate but to bring it to proportions more appropriate to our times.
Bill No. C-76 reads as follows:
An act to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960, with respect to representation of the provinces in the Senate and qualifications of senators.
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1.	Section 22 of the British North America Act, 1867, is amended by deleting the last paragraph thereto which at present reads as follows:
"In the case of Quebec, each of the twenty four senators representing that province shall be appointed for one of the twenty four electoral divisions of Lower Canada specified in schedule A to chapter one of the Consolidated Statutes of Canada."
Explanatory Note: "This paragraph, together with paragraph 6 of section 23, which it is also proposed

to delete, was inserted at the time of confederation to protect the English Protestant minority which was then located mainly in the eastern townships of the province of Quebec. Needless to say that no such provision has been inserted in the constitution to safeguard the French and Roman Catholic minorities of the other provinces.
However, as the population of the eastern townships is now mostly French Canadian, there is no need to perpetuate in the British North America Act such an obsolete provision.
Why should we keep in the statutes of the British North America Act a provision dating back to 1867, at a time when confederation comprised Upper and Lower Canada, while today our country includes ten provinces?
There is no such provision in any other Canadian province, except in the province of Quebec.
It seems to me that the federal parliament should remove that section which is altogether obsolete and outmoded.
Clause 2 of Bill C-76 reads as follows:
2.	Clause 23 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"23. The qualification of a senator shall be as follows:
(1)	He shall be of the full age of thirty years;
(2) He shall be a Canadian citizen;
(3) He shall be resident in the province for which he is appointed.
It seems to me that we have come to maturity and that we should repeal what is incorporated in clause 23 of the British North America Act, namely:
The qualifications of a senator shall be as follows:
(1)	He shall he at the full age of thirty years;
That qualification does not change.
(2)	He shall be either a natural-born subject of the Queen, or a subject of the Queen naturalized by an act of the parliament of Great Britain, or of the parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, or of the legislature of one of the provinces of Upper Canada, Lower Canada, Canada, Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick, before the union, or of the parliament of Canada, after the union;
Since this is the parliament of Canada after the union, after confederation, it seems to me that we should revert to more equitable requirements, that is to be Canadian citizens, which implies the whole thing in itself and proves that we are masters of our destiny and that we can decide for ourselves.
The third paragraph of that clause 23 reads as follows:
(3)	He shall be legally or equitably seized as freehold for his own use and benefit-
In simple terms, he must be the owner of property worth $4,000 over and above all his debts, mortgages, liabilities, etc.

(4)	His real and personal property shall be together worth four thousand dollars over and above his debts and liabilities:
(5)	He shall be resident in the province for which he is appointed.
Now, I come to the sixth paragraph and that is the one we want to eliminate. It reads as follows:
In the case of Quebec he shall have his real property qualification in the electoral division for which he is appointed, or shall be resident in that division."
Here is the explanatory note on that matter:
The main reason for the proposed change is that now that Canada is no longer a colony, only a Canadian should be qualified to be a senator. It is further suggested that if it is true that it is most difficult for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven, a poor man should not be prevented from entering the democratic Senate in the Kingdom of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the abrogation of clause 23(6) is proposed for reasons indicated in clause 1 of the bill. We are also suggesting that clauses 26, 27 and 28 of the said act be repealed and section 4 states:
That this act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1964, and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960 and this act may be cited together as the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1964.
Clauses 26, 27 and 28 which at the present time read as follows:
26.	If at any time on the recommendation of the Governor General the Queen thinks fit to direct that three or six members be added to the Senate, the Governor General may by summons to three or six qualified persons (as the case may be), representing equally the three divisions of Canada, add to the Senate accordingly.
Clause 27 reads as follows:
27.	In the case of such addition being at any time made, the Governor General shall not summon any person to the Senate, except upon a further like direction by the Queen on the like recommendation, to represent one of the three divisions until such division is represented by twenty four Senators and no more.
Clause 28 reads:
28.	The number of senators shall not at any time exceed seventy eight.
Since we never had to apply those clauses, why not repeal them? In fact, those clauses have never been used and we, nevertheless, tolerate them as it is provided that the number of senators should never exceed 78. At present, we have more than 78, we have 104. Therefore, clause 28 is outmoded and obsolete.

Today we have reached such a point of development and maturity that Canadian citizens, anyone of us from sea to sea, do not need to remain subject to another country, no matter how great, how noble or how powerful it may be. I say that honestly. I think that by Canadianizing all our institutions to the full, we are not offending the feelings of national unity which, I am sure, are shared by the majority of Canadian citizens.
Let us be truly and essentially Canadians everywhere, as regards facts and symbols.
Mr. Speaker, you saw how we respected the symbol of the British crown as represented by Her Majesty the Queen when she came to Canada. In the province of Quebec unfortunate incidents may have occurred, but such incidents were in no way a true reflection of the thinking in Quebec.
We respect the heads of state of all friendly countries. We particularly respect those of members of the commonwealth. But some day our constitutional evolution will be brought to completion, and to promote Canadianism is surely not to be against national unity. On the contrary, to see that this constitutional evolution reaches its ultimate goal shows a desire to do away with all ties of bondage or subjection to another country and thereby achieve true Canadianism. Such is the ideal of a young Canadian, and that is why I am happy about the new provision contained in my hon. friend's bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house are prepared to commend the purpose of the bill, which is to remove certain anomalies relating to the appointment of senators. The explanatory notes accompanying Bill No. C-76 set forth that a system of 24 electoral divisions, together with a property qualification of $4,000 worth of real estate in the electoral district for which the senator is appointed, was established for the province of Quebec and was designed to protect the English Protestant minority located for the most part in the eastern townships.
Although in 1867 the English Protestant minority was in the majority in 12 of the counties mentioned in schedule 2 of the British North America Act, I believe that by 1900 they retained a majority in only four of the counties. In practice, over the last 60 years the provisions which the bill seeks to eliminate have not been followed. In the province of Quebec senators have tended to be appointed from the districts of Montreal and Quebec, with little regard to the original intention of
British North America Act section 22, which was to assure appointment from each of the 24 divisions mentioned in schedule A of chapter 1 of the consolidated statutes of Canada.
Although this act providing for the protection of English Protestant privileges in the province of Quebec has in fact passed into our folklore, there are certain other Quebec English Protestant positions which have remained inflexible and stagnant, to the disadvantage of all Quebeckers and Canada as a whole. I refer specifically to one of our better known organizations in the province of Quebec, the Quebec Protestant board of education. Every society has its sacred cows and the English Protestants of Quebec certainly have theirs. Foremost among them is the Protestant board of education and its French teaching division.
The Quebec education act provides that the lieutenant governor in council may appoint by proclamation a Roman Catholic central board of examiners and a Protestant central board of examiners for the examination of candidates of each of the two religious beliefs for teachers' diplomas. This means in effect that each of the teaching professions in the Roman Catholic and Protestant systems is restricted to people of that particular faith, with the result that in the province of Quebec people who are called upon to teach the French language in English Protestant schools are for the most part English speaking and are all Protestant.
This has resulted, Mr. Speaker, in what I believe is one of the saddest situations that we face today in the province of Quebec, which is found in the fact that a considerable percentage of our English speaking population in the province of Quebec is not able to converse in French. All of these people who have been raised in the province of Quebec have studied French from grade 3 for five days a week in most cases. Yet by the time they finish high school 90 per cent of them at least are unable to converse in the French language. I submit this is the fault of the Protestant board of education and their inability to adjust to changing circumstances, and to make progress in the face of what has become a closed shop so far as the teachers are concerned.
